articles.title: In 2006, Beyoncé donated $2 million to build 42 apartments for people experiencing homelessness in Houston; the project became one of her earliest major housing initiatives
articles.summary: US News: Long before BeyGOOD became the name attached to Beyoncé's global charitable work, the singer was already putting significant money into community proj.
articles.body: Long before BeyGOOD became the name attached to Beyoncé's global charitable work, the singer was already putting significant money into community projects in Houston. According to the BeyGOOD foundation by Beyoncé, in 2006, she donated $2 million towards the construction of the Knowles-Temenos Place Apartments, a 42-unit housing complex for people experiencing homelessness. The contribution came soon after Hurricane Katrina, when Houston was dealing with the wider consequences of a disaster that had displaced thousands of people across the Gulf Coast.Beyoncé's support for relief efforts had already included a 2005 Fashion for Relief event, but the apartment project offered a different kind of response. It put money towards permanent housing rather than immediate supplies or emergency assistance. The development also followed years of community work involving Beyoncé, her family and Bread of Life. The donation predates the launch of BeyGOOD, which was established in 2013.Beyoncé donated $2 million in 2006 towards 42 apartments in HoustonThe Knowles-Temenos Place Apartments became a 42-unit housing complex for people without stable accommodation. Beyoncé contributed $2 million to the project, making it one of the largest individual charitable commitments associated with her early philanthropic work.The timing placed the development in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. The disaster had displaced families and placed enormous pressure on communities and organisations providing assistance across the region. Houston, in particular, became an important destination for people leaving areas affected by the storm.Beyoncé had already been involved in Katrina relief. In 2005, she took part in a Fashion for Relief event, with money raised going towards communities affected by the hurricane. The following year, her support took another form: housing.Beyoncé's Houston roots shaped her early philanthropyThe apartment project was not the beginning of Beyoncé's involvement with charitable causes. Her connection to community work in Houston went back further.In late 1990s, the Knowles-Rowland Center for Youth was established at Bread of Life, funded by Destiny's Child's first single and named after Beyoncé Knowles and Kelly Rowland. The centre initially served as a resource for teenagers before evolving into a shelter that could accommodate between 175 and 200 people which later became a disaster relief hub.Beyoncé and her family also established the Survivor Foundation in 2005 with a mission “Where There's A Will, We Help Make A Way.” Her parents, Mathew and Tina Knowles, her sister Solange Knowles and Kelly Rowland were among those involved in setting up the family charity.By the time the apartments were being developed, then, housing formed part of a broader pattern of work focused on people facing difficult circumstances.A permanent response to the housing crisisMuch of the immediate response to Hurricane Katrina involved food, clothing, money and other necessities. A housing development was different.The $2 million contribution was directed towards a permanent residential facility rather than a temporary relief distribution. The project created 42 individual units, giving the donation a physical presence in Houston that could continue serving residents after the initial period of emergency response had passed.There are few details available in the source material about the individual apartments, their residents or the precise arrangements under which the complex operated. What is established is the size of the donation, the number of units and the purpose of the development.Beyoncé's philanthropy moved beyond housingThe housing project was followed by other initiatives that addressed very different needs.In 2007, during The Beyoncé Experience tour, she worked with America's Second Harvest and Bread of Life to organise food banks at every tour stop. The effort was intended to help communities affected by famine.Two years later, during the North American leg of her ‘I AM... World Tour’, she partnered with Feeding America and General Mills on the Show Your Helping Hand campaign. Reportedly, the initiative aimed to deliver more than 3.5 million meals to local food banks and also raised money for hunger relief.Her charitable activity also moved into employment and rehabilitation. After researching her role in the 2008 film Cadillac Records, Beyoncé donated her entire salary from the film to Phoenix House, a drug and alcohol treatment organisation. That support helped establish the Beyoncé Cosmetology Center, which provided job training for people recovering from addiction.BeyGOOD came later in 2013Beyoncé formally launched BeyGOOD in 2013 during the Mrs. Carter Show World Tour. The organisation would eventually become a major vehicle for her philanthropic programmes, covering areas such as education, disaster relief, economic opportunity, health and community support.The 2006 apartment donation predates BeyGOOD by several years. It therefore belongs to an earlier period of her charitable work, when support was being delivered through family organisations, partnerships and individual projects rather than through the later foundation structure.Beyoncé's housing work returned to Houston in 2026Housing would eventually appear again in Beyoncé's philanthropic record.As reported, in 2026, Beyoncé and Kelly Rowland invested $8.4 million in the Knowles-Rowland House, a 31-unit permanent housing development with supportive services for people experiencing homelessness. The project was built on the site of the original Knowles-Rowland Center for Youth and was scheduled to open in 2026.The later development is separate from the 2006 Knowles-Temenos Place Apartments. The two projects are nevertheless part of a longer history of housing-related work connected with Beyoncé and her family.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Himachal under monsoon fury: 259 dead, 150 roads cut off, losses cross Rs 1,200 crore in last 64 days
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Monsoon rains have claimed 259 lives and caused damage worth more than Rs 1,200 crore across Himachal Pradesh in just 64 days, according to.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Monsoon rains have claimed 259 lives and caused damage worth more than Rs 1,200 crore across Himachal Pradesh in just 64 days, according to State Emergency Operations Centre (SEOC) data. Meanwhile, the latest spell of rain has severely affected connectivity, with 150 roads currently blocked across Himachal Pradesh.Mandi has reported the highest number of closures at 78, followed by Shimla with 30. Fresh rainfall has also disrupted power and water supplies across the hill state.Essential services have also been hit. As many as 374 distribution transformer regions (DTRs) are out of service, affecting power supply across several districts. Mandi has recorded 128 affected DTRs, followed by Shimla with 84 and Kullu with 81.The water supply network has also suffered disruption, with 40 schemes currently affected. Hamirpur accounts for 23 of the disrupted schemes, while Shimla has reported 17.The mounting disruptions come against the backdrop of a deadly monsoon season that has claimed 259 lives between June 30 and September 1. Of the total fatalities, 106 were caused by rain and disaster-related incidents, including 18 deaths in landslides and 13 due to drowning. Another 153 people died in road accidents during the period.Lahaul and Spiti, the high-altitude tribal district, recorded 15 deaths linked to monsoon-related disasters.The rains have also inflicted extensive damage on public and private infrastructure, with the cumulative losses estimated at Rs 1,202.64 crore. The Public Works Department bore the biggest share of the damage at more than Rs 914 crore, while the Jal Shakti Vibhag reported losses exceeding Rs 258 crore.The disaster has completely damaged 460 houses and resulted in the deaths of 460 animals, the SEOC data showed.State government departments and field agencies are now carrying out restoration operations in affected districts, working to reopen blocked roads and restore power and water supply.With the monsoon continuing to disrupt normal life, the latest figures underline the scale of the crisis facing Himachal Pradesh, where hundreds of lives have been lost and critical infrastructure has suffered extensive damage in just over two months.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Duke University began exposing North Carolina forest plots to elevated CO2; after 10 years, loblolly pines produced about 20% more biomass
articles.summary: US News: A decade-long study by Duke University reveals that loblolly pines exposed to 1.5 times normal CO2 levels show a 20% biomass increase, highlighting the complexities of carbon sequestration in forests.
articles.body: In a forest outside Durham, North Carolina, Duke University spent over a decade testing a simple question: what happens when mature trees grow in air containing relatively more carbon dioxide than they normally experience? The long-running Free-Air Carbon Enrichment (FACE) experiment exposed forest plots to elevated carbon levels under open-air conditions instead of enclosing the trees in chambers. By 2007, researchers reported that after a study of over 10 years, the treated, loblolly-pine-dominated plots had produced around 20% more biomass on average than matched plots receiving ambient carbon dioxide levels.In 1994, a prototype FACE plot at Duke began receiving elevated CO2, while a completely replicated experiment began in August 1996 with three elevated CO2 plots and three controls. Following this, the facility later expanded to four elevated and four control plots that were described in Duke’s 2007 report. Therefore, 1997 is associated with the four-plot configuration used in the long-term study instead of being the absolute beginning of CO2 enrichment at Duke Forest.After nearly a decade of elevated CO2 exposure, the treated forest landscapes had accumulated around one-fifth more biomass on average. The experiment also showed why the average could not be interpreted as a universal response, because localised soil conditions and resource constraints have a huge impact on how the trees synthesise the changed atmosphere from plot to plot.A higher atmospheric CO2 experiment was conducted by The Duke FACEThe Duke FACE facility was built in a loblolly pine plantation that was established in 1983. Loblolly pine (Pinus taeda) was the dominant tree, making the site useful for studying species widely distributed and commercially important across the southeastern United States. Rather than growing seedlings inside a greenhouse, researchers raised the carbon dioxide concentration around standing trees while allowing the forest to remain exposed to natural environmental conditions.The FACE system used rings of towers fitted with computer-controlled valves to release additional CO2 around the plots. Operating across these matched treatment and control parcels, the system adjusted output to reflect 1.5 times the CO2 concentration of the period, while the experimental literature more precisely describes the target as approximately 200 parts per million above ambient.The elevated-CO2 lands were maintained at concentrations around 550-570 parts per million during the experiment, depending on the ambient conditions and the treatment protocol. Therefore, the trees experienced higher carbon dioxide while continuing to grow in the open forest, with natural variation in temperature, rainfall, soil moisture and competition.The goal of the experiment was to see how additional atmospheric carbon affected biomass production, carbon storage, water usage and nutrient cycling. Those questions became increasingly important as scientists considered whether forests could absorb any of the additional CO2 entering the atmosphere from human activities.The 20% increase came with a major qualificationDuke reported that trees in the elevated-CO2 plots produced about 20% more biomass on average than those in the control plots. The researchers found a growth increase of only around 5-10% in some areas, compared with increases approaching 40% in others.The difference was closely related to resources available to the trees, as where water and nitrogen were scarce, the extra CO2 produced little additional growth. Where both resources were abundant, the response was much larger. This result indicated that carbon dioxide was only one part of the growth equation because trees also needed enough water and nutrients to turn the additional carbon available from photosynthesis into new tissue.The finding complicated the idea that forests could simply be used to bank excess atmospheric carbon. If rising carbon dioxide coincides with reduced water availability, Duke researchers cautioned, the increase in carbon sequestration could be much smaller or even disappear. A similar constraint applied to nutrients: increasing CO2 alone did not guarantee that a forest would continue to produce proportionally more biomass indefinitely. Thus, the researchers warned against treating the 20% average as a universal prediction for every forest, as this was only an experimental result from a particular loblolly-pine-dominated ecosystem, under particular soil, climate and resource conditions.It is worth noting that earlier observations by the same facility had already shown that the response could change with time. In 2005, Duke reported that pine growth under elevated CO2 had been substantially higher in several early years, with the largest increase reaching 25% in 1999. That early response did not mean the stimulation would continue indefinitely.What a decade of extra CO2 elevation revealedThe Duke experiment offered a more complicated picture than the simple idea that higher atmospheric CO2 automatically means proportionally larger carbon storage. The trees responded with 20% more biomass on average in the treated plots. But the response varied significantly with water and nitrogen availability, and the destination of that additional carbon mattered when assessing long-term sequestration.Furthermore, the experiment showcased the value of studying mature vegetation under open-air conditions, with the FACE technology allowing researchers to raise CO2 without sealing the forest inside an enclosure, thus preserving many interactions that occur in an actual ecosystem.Later research continues to refine the picture. A study examining trees harvested from the Duke FACE site found that the plots exposed to elevated CO2 from 1996 to 2010 contained around 21% more aboveground biomass when standard diameter-based biomass equations were used; accounting for changes in tree form increased the estimated treatment effect to around 27%. These later measurements are consistent with the general finding that elevated carbon dioxide increased wood volume, while demonstrating that the initial 10-year estimates remained highly conservative.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2010, Texas researchers injected dyes into 6 caves to map the Edwards Aquifer; groundwater crossed faults at up to 5,300 metres per day, revealing rapid flow paths
articles.summary: US News: A groundbreaking study from Texas reveals that groundwater in the Edwards Aquifer moves astonishingly fast, raising concerns about pollution risks. Researchers injected fluorescent dye into caves and monitored its movement, uncovering links between different aquifers and potential contamination pathways. This vital information is crucial for protecting drinking water supplies in the region.
articles.body: In 2010, the Edwards Aquifer Authority conducted a series of tracer tests in northern Bexar County, injecting nontoxic fluorescent dyes into six caves and monitoring 32 public and private wells to trace groundwater flowpaths. The tests recorded apparent groundwater velocities of up to 5,300 metres per day in the Panther Springs Creek groundwater basin. What they found was startling. In some spots, groundwater raced through the underground limestone at up to 5,300 metres per day, crossing major geological faults along the way, results that reshaped how officials think about protecting a water source that millions of people rely on every single day.Dye dropped into six caves near San AntonioThe Edwards Aquifer recharge zone in northern Bexar County is a karst landscape, where groundwater can move through fractures, conduits and other openings in limestone. Instead of soaking slowly through sand and gravel, water in this region moves through a maze of caves, sinkholes and dissolved limestone passages carved out over millions of years, a type of formation known as karst. To map how water actually travels through that maze, researchers injected fluorescent dyes into six caves within the San Antonio segment of the aquifer, aiming to trace flow paths and estimate velocities in the Panther Springs Creek groundwater basin in northern Bexar County. Detecting where the dye eventually surfaced required a wide net. The monitoring array consisted of 32 public and private wells, including irrigation wells at a local golf club and public water supply wells serving nearby neighbourhoods. This scale of testing meant the team could see not just whether the caves connected to nearby wells, but how quickly and along what routes.Water moved faster than anyone expectedThe results showed just how quickly contamination could spread if it ever entered the system at the wrong spot. Groundwater velocities to one particular well ranged from 1,100 to 5,300 metres per day, while velocities to other wells where dye was detected ranged from 13 to 2,330 metres per day. Just as significant was where that water was travelling from. The dye showed that flow paths between the caves and the monitored wells crossed several faults running northeast to southwest and that faults with displacement of up to 104 metres did not block the movement of groundwater at all. The tracer results also indicated a hydraulic connection between the Edwards Aquifer and the upper part of the underlying Glen Rose Formation within the Upper Trinity Aquifer in the study area. A 2019 Geological Society of America chapter reviewing tracer testing across the Edwards Aquifer shows how widely groundwater velocities can vary between locations. In the Barton Springs segment, earlier tracer tests measured velocities of 915 to 9,150 metres per day, while the 2010 Panther Springs Creek study recorded apparent velocities of 13 to 5,300 metres per day.A warning for a water supply that serves millionsPerhaps the most sobering part of the study had nothing to do with a cave at all. Researchers also released dye at a plain patch of ground with no visible karst features, no sinkhole, no cave entrance, and nothing to suggest it was connected to anything below. Dye still turned up in nearby wells within weeks, showing that vulnerable ground is not limited to the obvious, dramatic-looking openings that most people associate with karst landscapes. That has real consequences for a region where groundwater doubles as the primary drinking supply.A separate study by the US Geological Survey on a nearby well field found that karst features act as fast pathways for contaminants, with almost half the water reaching one public supply well estimated to be less than two years old, leaving little time for natural processes to filter out anything harmful before it reaches a tap. Tracer studies had already been used elsewhere in the Edwards Aquifer for years. The Barton Springs/Edwards Aquifer Conservation District and the City of Austin conducted groundwater tracing in the Barton Springs segment from 1996 through 2000. The 2010 Edwards Aquifer Authority study added a separate set of observations from the Panther Springs Creek basin in northern Bexar County. The findings reinforce why protecting the recharge zone matters: the study showed that groundwater can move rapidly through the subsurface and that contamination risks are not limited to places with obvious caves or sinkholes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: MPSC paper leak row: Chairman Vivek Bhimanwar says leak happened before he took charge
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) chairman Vivek Bhimanwar has said the question paper leak in the Drug Inspector (Group-B) examina.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) chairman Vivek Bhimanwar has said the question paper leak in the Drug Inspector (Group-B) examination took place before he took charge of the recruitment body, amid demands for his resignation.In a statement issued on Wednesday, Bhimanwar said the incident relating to the Drug Inspector examination occurred in January 2026, while he took charge as MPSC chief on February 18 and assumed office on March 3, news agency PTI reported.“It is necessary to take into account the facts regarding the period of the incident,” Bhimanwar said, referring to allegations being levelled against him over the paper leak.He said the MPSC had taken serious note of the alleged question paper leak and lodged a complaint, adding that police were investigating the matter.The Mumbai police have arrested seven people, including Rutuja Patil, who had secured seventh rank in the examination, in connection with the case.According to Bhimanwar, the commission has also constituted a high-level internal committee to recommend preventive and security measures to ensure that such incidents are not repeated, PTI reported.The state government has separately formed a high-level committee to suggest necessary improvements in the overall examination process, he said.Several important reforms have been initiated to make the examination and recruitment system more robust and secure, particularly as the commission has been entrusted with increased recruitment responsibilities, he said.“Safeguarding the commission’s high traditions, impartiality and credibility, and providing millions of candidates a fair and equal opportunity, is my constitutional responsibility. I am committed to discharging this responsibility with complete transparency, impartiality and integrity,” he said.Bhimanwar said elected representatives, candidates and citizens had every right to raise questions and express concerns regarding public examinations.“I welcome such questions in a democratic system. However, any serious allegation should be assessed only on the basis of facts, official records and evidence,” he said.He appealed that sensitive issues involving the future of millions of young candidates in public recruitment processes should not be turned into personal allegations or political controversies, PTI reported.Allegations have surfaced on social media claiming that Bhimanwar had a role in the paper leak episode.The recruitment process for Drug Inspectors had been initiated through an advertisement issued on July 29, 2025.The screening examination was conducted offline at six divisional headquarters across Maharashtra on March 22 this year.The result was declared on June 12, after which 506 candidates were found eligible for the interview stage, the commission had said earlier.Of these, 488 candidates appeared for interviews conducted between July 1 and 22.After completion of the interviews, the MPSC published a provisional general merit list comprising 488 candidates, including 485 candidates found eligible for appointment and three declared ineligible, it said.However, complaints concerning the conduct of the screening examination were received by the commission between July 22 and 26 through e-mail from some candidates as well as public representatives.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: 34,000 cans stolen: US company offers reward to recover 40,000-pound beer load
articles.summary: US News: US Beer maker Pabst Blue Ribbon has offered a cash reward for information leading to the recovery of a truckload of beer stolen from a warehouse in So.
articles.body: US Beer maker Pabst Blue Ribbon has offered a cash reward for information leading to the recovery of a truckload of beer stolen from a warehouse in Southern California, turning the unusual theft into a social media appeal.The company said about 40,000 pounds (18,000 kg) of beer was taken from an Anheuser-Busch distribution centre in Montclair, around 60 km east of Los Angeles, on August 17. Pabst urged whoever took the shipment to return it within a countdown period, promising “no questions asked”.“We don’t fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honorable way,” the company said in an Instagram post, while adding that it was “deadly serious” about recovering the shipment.Pabst senior director of integrated marketing operations Paul Myers told CBS News that police believe a person impersonated the legitimate party due to collect the beer and drove away with it. The company is offering a cash reward worth half the value of the stolen products, Myers said.Police said there were actually two separate thefts from the warehouse on the same day. In the first incident, around $45,000 worth of beer bound for Tucson, Arizona, was collected but never delivered. About an hour later, a purported subcontractor used fraudulent documents to collect another shipment valued at around $25,000.A police report cited by the Los Angeles Times said roughly 34,000 cans of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer, packed into more than 1,500 cases, were stolen. Police have valued the two thefts at about $70,000 and are investigating whether they were part of the same cargo-theft operation.Pabst initially took a humorous approach on social media, posting that the “beer is getting warmer, trail is getting colder”, before shifting to a more serious appeal for help finding the truck.The theft also drew a playful response from KitKat US, which referenced a similar incident in March when a truck carrying about 12 tonnes of its Formula 1-themed chocolate bars was stolen in Italy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Not charity': Nepal seeks compensation from India, US, China for deadly flood
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal has launched a diplomatic push to seek climate-related compensation from major greenhouse gas emitters, including India, the US and China, as th.
articles.body: Nepal has launched a diplomatic push to seek climate-related compensation from major greenhouse gas emitters, including India, the US and China, as the country grapples with the devastating aftermath of deadly flash floods.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal said the Himalayan nation contributes "virtually negligible" greenhouse gas emissions but is bearing a disproportionate share of the consequences of climate change, including rapid glacier melt and extreme mountain disasters."We are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create. The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change," he said in an interview with Kantipur TV, excerpts of which were published by The Kathmandu Post.Khanal said Nepal was shifting its diplomatic approach from seeking "aid" to demanding "justice and compensation"."This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability," he said, adding that Nepal would raise the issue "with absolute firmness and clarity" at international forums.As per news agency PTI, the foreign minister identified China, the US and India as the world's three largest greenhouse gas emitters and said they had a "historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.""This is a matter of civilisational survival. If our Himalayan glaciers disappear, the water security of over two billion people in South Asia dependent on rivers like the Ganges and the Trishuli will be permanently compromised. We are advocating not just for Nepal, but for the survival of South Asian civilisation," he said.Nepal has also formally approached the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, seeking urgent financial assistance following the Bhotekoshi River basin flash flood.A letter jointly signed by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Forests and Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary said the disaster had caused extensive economic and non-economic losses that exceeded Nepal's immediate response capacity.'India is powerful and like God to us': What Nepal flood survivors saidMeanwhile, survivors of the August 26 flash floods have been relying on immediate humanitarian assistance, including support from neighbouring India.In Nuwakot, the Nepal-Bharat Maitri Bhawan, which houses an Ayurveda and Alternative Hospital rebuilt with financial assistance from the Embassy of India after the 2015 earthquake, has become a refuge for displaced residents.Hospital chief Dr Narendra Prasad Giri said more than 100 displaced people were staying at the facility each night, while medical teams were also being sent to nearby shelters."This building is a post-earthquake reconstruction, and it was assisted financially by the Embassy of India. This building is a core support for the people. Many devastated people who were rescued from there, we brought them here and treated, and their health is now stable," Giri told ANI.One survivor, recalling how floodwaters swept him away while he was trying to save his goats, said hospital staff reassured him after he was injured."Here, the doctors and sisters (nurses) told me, 'Don't cry, we will save you, treat your wounds, apply medicine, and make you fine right here.' They are treating me and helping me; I'm receiving good care and facilities," he said.Expressing gratitude for India's assistance, he told ANI, "Indian government is like our neighboring nation, a friend. Now that this happened in Nepal, the Indian government has given us a lot of support. India is powerful and like God to us."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Why did you sell it?’: Sons beat up parents in Pune over land dispute
articles.summary: PUNE: Two brothers allegedly assaulted their elderly parents with wooden sticks after getting angry over the sale of land owned by their mother in Mah.
articles.body: PUNE: Two brothers allegedly assaulted their elderly parents with wooden sticks after getting angry over the sale of land owned by their mother in Maharashtra's Pune district, police said on Wednesday.The incident took place on the evening of August 30 at Tarangwadi village in Indapur tehsil.According to a complaint filed by 65-year-old farmer Tukaram Raut, he and his ailing wife, Anjana, were out for a walk when their two sons, who live separately with their families in Malwadi, arrived in a car.The brothers allegedly questioned the couple about why land registered in Anjana's name had been sold before attacking them with wooden sticks.Tukaram suffered injuries to his back, face, thighs and shoulder, while his wife sustained injuries to her wrist and waist. The accused also allegedly abused the couple and threatened to kill them if the land deal was not cancelled, police said.Locals gathered at the spot and alerted the police, following which the injured couple was taken to the Sub-District Hospital in Indapur for treatment.A case has been registered against the two brothers at Indapur police station under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Meet Connor Gibson, a 22-year-old Tennessee engineer using 3D printing to make free dentures for Americans who are not able to afford them
articles.summary: US News: 3D printing has come a long way over the years. No longer is it solely used for printing figures and props for D&D campaigns, but it is now expand.
articles.body: 3D printing has come a long way over the years. No longer is it solely used for printing figures and props for D&D campaigns, but it is now expanding to take space in all kinds of places, including your mouth. According to a CNN report, a 22-year-old engineer Connor Gibson, is using the 3D printing technique to make free dentures for people who may not be able to afford them. The Tennessee native is working with Remote Area Medical, helping turn a process that once took three months into one that takes only a few hours.Gibson volunteered with the nonprofit while studying engineering at Walters State Community College. He was instantly inspired by the organisation's mission to help the country's poor and was determined to find a way to improve the speed at which dentures could be delivered.Interestingly, he had no background in dentistry and not much knowledge of 3D printing. But he taught himself all about dental anatomy and digital design, learning the depths of the software needed to manufacture custom dentures based on every patient's scans. “Honestly, if you told me three years ago, this is what I would be doing, I would have called you crazy,” he told CNN.A crazy weekendOut of all the things you could spend your weekends doing, getting customised dentures made is now one. Gibson now works as RAM's digital technology manager with a mobile office loaded with two 3D printers that run round-the-clock on weekends. He has printed as many as 35 sets of dentures in a single weekend. The non-profit organisation based out of Rockford, Tennessee, provides free dental, vision and medical care through volunteer-powered mobile clinics across US.“Never, ever, in school did they say, ‘You can design something that could change someone’s life like a denture,’” Gibson told the outlet. “It’s not something immediately on someone’s mind when they’re thinking, ‘Oh, I’m going into engineering.’”“Mirror moments” is what Gibson calls the experience of watching someone with a freshly printed set of dentures see their new, beautiful mouth of teeth in the mirror for the first time, with some openly weeping at a sight they never imagined they would get to see again. “Something that I was able to have a hand in makes a grown man burst into tears,” Gibson said, reflecting on the first patient. “To see that raw, human emotion and just know that I played a change in this person’s life … it’s very humbling, and I’m beyond blessed.”“Since then, it’s all just like fireworks every weekend. That’s what we’re striving for — to get more and more of those mirror moments. It’s something you can’t truly describe unless you’re there.”In the US, about 72 million adults, roughly 27% of the population, do not have dental insurance. Even for those who have Medicare, the US federal health insurance program primarily for people 65 and older, in most cases it doesn’t cover dental services like routine cleanings, fillings or items like dentures and implants. He is a dental saviour at a time when millions of Americans lack dental insurance and when Medicare lacks dental coverage for some.Continuing a legacyRemote Area Medical has served over 1 million patients and provided nearly $240 million in care since its founding in 1985, thanks to the charity’s 230,000 volunteers. It was founded by the late Stan Brock, the captivating British cowboy who co-starred in “Mutual of Omaha’s Wild Kingdom” television series in the 1960s and ’70s, before making it his life mission to provide free healthcare to underserved communities across the United States.It was the documentary on Brock that first inspired Gibson. He saw the film at a movie theatre in 2023 with his father. “That movie really opened my eyes when it comes to where our nation is right now,” he said.RAM’s CEO Chris Hall first joined the charity in 2013. At the time, the organisation held about 12 events a year. In 2026, RAM plans to host more than 90 “full-scale medical, dental, and vision clinics.” “The goal for us is to make someone’s day better,” Hall told CNN.He said Gibson embodies everything about Brock and his legacy. “Connor never had the opportunity to meet Stan,” Hall said. “But if Stan was to meet Connor, I think Stan would see someone who truly has the ability to change the world, someone who has passion to help other people.”Gibson's story has brought in more support for the organisation. A manufacturer of 3D printers reached out, Hall said, about donating newer and better machines that will give RAM a fleet of three mobile dental units, instead of its current one lab. That will allow RAM and Gibson to make over 100 dentures in a single weekend, tripling the number of “mirror moments.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: USCIS can now seek credit information of a green card sponsor from agencies
articles.summary: US News: The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has made an overnight change to the Form I-864, which is the ‘Affidavit of Support’ filed by those.
articles.body: The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has made an overnight change to the Form I-864, which is the ‘Affidavit of Support’ filed by those sponsoring family members for a green card. From Aug 31, only the new version will be accepted for filings submitted on or after this date – no grace period is available for continued use of the older form.American Immigration Lawyers’ Association (AILA) points out a notable change in the new version. “It includes a privacy release that authorizes USCIS to request credit related information (about the sponsor) from one or more consumer reporting agencies.”“If a sponsor has a credit or security freeze on their consumer or credit report file, USCIS may not be able to access the information necessary to assess the sufficiency of Form I-864. To avoid any delays, a sponsor should expeditiously respond to any requests made to release a credit or security freeze,” states AILA.Consumers typically place a freeze with the major credit-reporting agencies to help prevent unauthorized accounts from being opened in their name. A freeze does not erase or damage a person's credit history; it simply limits who can access the report while the freeze is in place.Manifest Law has posted insights on this development. Ana Gabriela Urizar, immigration attorney states that while Form I-864 was already a binding contract to support the immigrant financially, the addition made is that “USCIS can go straight to the credit bureaus to check your numbers, so sponsors should make sure their income and asset documentation actually matches what's on file before they sign."Immigration attorneys point out that the new form does not specify any credit score that must be met. USCIS has also not announced that every sponsor will undergo a credit inquiry or that every sponsor's credit score will routinely be reviewed. While the new form does not state that a low credit score, high credit-card balances, missed payments, or a prior bankruptcy automatically disqualifies someone from being a financial sponsor, immigration attorneys add that it remains to be seen how USCIS will use its authority.Form I-864 has traditionally focused on the sponsor's financial ability through information such as: Household size; current annual income and household income; federal tax returns; income and asset documentation to name a few.The basic financial requirement has not been replaced by a credit-score requirement. Generally, a sponsor must demonstrate income at or above 125% of the applicable federal poverty guidelines. To illustrate – this translates into $41,250 for a household of four members in the Washington DC area. With USCIS now having an additional avenue to seek financial information about the sponsor it makes the Form I-864 review broader.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mecca Pact and Bangladesh: Why Dhaka is keeping the door open to 'Islamic Nato'
articles.summary: South Asia News: In August, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye unveiled what has informally been dubbed the “Islamic Nato”. Named after Makkah, Islam’s holiest city, .
articles.body: In August, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye unveiled what has informally been dubbed the “Islamic Nato”. Named after Makkah, Islam’s holiest city, the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement or simply the Mecca pact—is based on the principle that an armed attack on one member would be considered an attack on all three, similar to Nato's Article 5.Since the pact was announced, Bangladesh has signalled that it could join the grouping. Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has not publicly commented on the possibility, but his foreign minister and junior ministers have said Dhaka is “interested” and would respond “positively” if invited.Against that backdrop, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman’s invitation to Tarique Rahman to visit the Kingdom is also likely to attract added attention.What lies behind Dhaka’s interest in the pact is less clear. But several factors could be shaping its thinking.Mecca pact: A different security calculus for DhakaOver the years, Bangladesh, as a member of the Non-Aligned Movement, has followed a policy of not taking sides with major powers during conflicts. Experts also point out that, unlike the three founding members of the Mecca security alliance, Bangladesh does not face the kind of immediate external military threat confronting some of the pact’s founding members.Others have raised concerns about the agreement’s “collective security” principle, arguing that it could draw Dhaka into a war not of its own making.Why, then, are Bangladesh’s ministers talking about joining the tri-nation agreement?According to Professor Sreeradha Datta, who teaches International Affairs at OP Jindal Global University, Bangladesh would definitely want to leverage the interest of other countries in it.“I think right now, Bangladesh would like to have a reach beyond the (immediate) region. And if others are getting interested in Bangladesh, why wouldn't they leverage it?” Professor Datta told The Times of India.Besides, the three countries would offer Bangladesh different advantages. Pakistan brings military and strategic weight in South Asia and is the only Muslim-majority country with nuclear weapons; Türkiye offers high-tech defence capabilities and technology, as well as Nato’s second-largest military; and Saudi Arabia brings economic and diplomatic weight.Taken together, these ties could give Dhaka access to a wider range of strategic, military and economic partnerships, while allowing it to expand its reach beyond the immediate region. In return, Bangladesh would bring a sizable military to the alliance and give the grouping a member strategically located on the Bay of Bengal.The 'Muslim family' argumentOn August 30, a day before the alliance’s first meeting in Türkiye's Istanbul, Bangladesh’s foreign affairs minister Khalilur Rahman reiterated a point he had made previously: that joining the Mecca pact was a matter for the world’s “Muslim family."Bangladesh would positively consider joining the Mecca defence, if invited... It is an internal matter of “our Muslim family” with no scope for others to be concerned about itThe minister's framing of the agreement, therefore, allows Dhaka to present its interest partly through the lens of shared religious identity, even though formal membership would carry significant strategic obligations.Professor Datta, however, also pointed to Bangladesh’s longstanding interests with these nations.“They (Bangladesh) have a lot of interests like energy and remittance and many other interests with these countries. In any case, it has a very growing relationship with Turkiye and has always had very good engagements with them,” she said.Meanwhile, Pakistan claimed after the bloc's Istanbul meeting that several other Muslim-majority states had expressed interest in joining the pact, suggesting that the grouping could expand while remaining exclusively Muslim-majority.A calculation for domestic politics?Bangladesh ministers have repeatedly asserted that the Tarique Rahman government’s approach to the Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Türkiye military alliance is guided by its “Bangladesh First” policy, with “national interests at its core.”Foreign minister Khalilur Rahman, for instance, stated that Bangladesh will “never bow its head to anyone again” and that the current government has “buried the subservient foreign policy.”Professor Datta said there is also a domestic political dimension, with the incumbent government potentially seeking to appeal to a constituency that remains deeply invested in the “Hasina factor.”“Given the tense relationship with India, the domestic constituency is of course very important and there is a large constituency that obviously considers the Hasina factor very strongly,” she said, referring to former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was ousted in a student-led movement in 2024 and has been living in New Delhi since then.Against continuing political hostility towards Hasina, Dhaka’s signalling on the pact could also carry a domestic political dividend, particularly among constituencies supportive of a more independent foreign-policy posture.Therefore, the government’s signalling on the Mecca pact can be politically useful, whether Bangladesh ultimately joins the alliance or not.The India factor in Bangladesh's calculusAs an immediate neighbour, India cannot afford to ignore Bangladesh’s strategic choices. The two countries share a more than 4,000-km-long border spanning five Indian states, making Dhaka central to New Delhi’s security and strategic calculus.But diplomatic tensions, with the non-extradition of Sheikh Hasina at the centre of the dispute, continue to strain bilateral ties. The former prime minister was convicted in absentia and sentenced to death for crimes against humanity linked to deaths during her administration’s crackdown on protests, although she has rejected the conviction as a “political witch hunt.”For his part, Tarique Rahman, since becoming prime minister in February, has visited several Asian countries, including China, but is yet to visit India. That he is yet to visit India despite invitations from New Delhi reflects the continuing sensitivity in bilateral ties.However, New Delhi has repeatedly signalled its interest in hosting him. Could Bangladesh’s signalling on the Mecca Pact, therefore, be a message to India that Dhaka is keeping its options open?Professor Datta sees Dhaka’s approach as a way of telling major powers, including India, that Bangladesh has other options, so that it need not depend on any one external power.“They're telling everybody, including India, that we have other options... It's more of a both domestic and external messaging that 'We (Bangladesh) have other options so that we don't have to depend on one particular external power',” she said.Additionally, Bangladesh knows that if it joins the alliance, two of its three partners would be countries whose ties with India have faced significant strains — Pakistan and Türkiye.In fact, Bangladesh-Pakistan ties had already improved significantly under the Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration in Dhaka, well before the Mecca pact emerged. The rapprochement included reciprocal security visits, raising eyebrows in New Delhi.For Bangladesh, therefore, simply signalling interest in the agreement could send a message to India that it is considering other strategic options while the relationship remains strained.What would Bangladesh’s Mecca Pact membership meanFor Dhaka, a formal membership would mean taking on the commitments that come with a collective-defence arrangement. That would mark a significant shift for a country that has traditionally been reluctant to enter formal military alliances.But Professor Datta does not expect Bangladesh to become a direct member of the alliance, at least for now. Some form of association, she believes, could be more plausible.“I don't think, at this point, Bangladesh is going to join the alliance as a direct member. In some form of association, maybe an observer status, but they will certainly have other considerations.”One of those “considerations,” she says, is likely to be domestic opinion towards Pakistan. While official engagement between Dhaka and Islamabad has grown, a formal defence alliance could be politically difficult to sell at home as it may not go down well with the public, given the history between the two nations.For now, therefore, it remains to be seen whether Dhaka will restrict itself to signalling interest or go beyond it and pursue some form of formal association with the alliance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US-Iran war flares up again: How far can Tehran go in retaliation?
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran fired missiles at US assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq on Tuesday night after the United States launched a fresh wave of attacks on Iran.
articles.body: Iran fired missiles at US assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq on Tuesday night after the United States launched a fresh wave of attacks on Iran. The strikes marked a new escalation in the six-month conflict. Tehran now faces several options for retaliation, including expanding attacks on Gulf states, disrupting oil shipments and targeting Western interests.The renewed US offensive marks a fresh escalation in a conflict that has already disrupted shipping and energy supplies across the Middle East. Tehran now faces a choice between widening attacks across the region, tightening pressure on Gulf oil exports or taking the confrontation directly to Western interests.Expand attacks on Gulf statesIran could intensify strikes against US military facilities and other targets in Gulf states and Jordan, where it has repeatedly launched attacks since the war began on February 28.While US bases have been the primary targets, Iranian strikes have also hit energy infrastructure. A broader campaign against upstream oil and gas facilities could create a sharper shock for global energy markets and put additional political pressure on the Trump administration.Iran could also target power generation and water desalination plants in Gulf states. Such attacks would pose a significant threat to countries that are key US allies as well as major financial hubs.Threaten Gulf oil suppliesOne of Tehran’s most consequential options would be to further disrupt the movement of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Mohsen Rezaei, the former Revolutionary Guards chief and secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has threatened to shut down oil exports if the economic pressure on Tehran continues.He said if the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported through the Strait of Hormuz or from anywhere in the Persian Gulf.The threat carries weight because the strait has already been severely disrupted. Iranian attacks and threats against shipping have largely halted traffic through the waterway, which carried around a fifth of global energy supplies before the conflict.Some tankers have continued to pass through the strait in recent weeks, but volumes remain very low. Missile, drone and speedboat attacks, along with threats against vessels, have repeatedly driven up oil prices during the six-month conflict.Any further disruption could send another shock through global energy markets.Tighten pressure in the Red SeaIran could also rely on its regional allies to increase pressure on shipping routes outside the Persian Gulf.The Iran-backed Houthis have already restricted Red Sea shipping through attacks and threats against vessels, including warnings over Saudi shipping that carries crude towards Asia through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.The disruption is increasingly affecting shipping decisions. Chinese shipping companies are now rerouting vessels away from Bab el-Mandeb, according to industry sources.Further attacks could heighten concerns in the oil market. Recent incidents include an attack targeting a vessel near Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil terminal at Yanbu and a drone strike near the Suez Canal.Take the fight to the WestIran could also seek to retaliate beyond the Middle East through cyber operations or covert attacks.Western countries are largely beyond the range of Iran’s principal missile systems, but the Revolutionary Guards have historically used alternative methods to target adversaries.Britain has said Iran-linked hackers shut down a small electricity station, while US officials have said Tehran was likely behind cyberattacks on water plants in Minnesota. Iran has not commented on those allegations.Western security services have also accused Iran of recruiting people to carry out attacks or assassination attempts in Western countries. Tehran has denied those accusations.With direct US-Iran fighting now resuming, Tehran’s response could therefore extend well beyond the battlefield. Any decision to target Gulf energy infrastructure, choke shipping through Hormuz, widen attacks in the Red Sea or strike Western interests would risk turning the latest escalation into a broader regional and global crisis.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Sita’s character greater than Rama’s’: DK Shivakumar urges women to take leadership roles
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Karnataka chief minister D K Shivakumar on Wednesday invoked Sita’s character in the Ramayana to highlight women’s strength and sacrifices,.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Karnataka chief minister D K Shivakumar on Wednesday invoked Sita’s character in the Ramayana to highlight women’s strength and sacrifices, saying women could play a decisive role in the state’s economic growth and should step into leadership positions from gram panchayats to Parliament.Speaking after inaugurating the fifth edition of ‘Together We Grow-International Women Entrepreneurship Day’, organised by the Ubuntu Consortium of Women Entrepreneurs Association, Shivakumar said women who built businesses despite challenges were role models."In the Ramayana, Sita's character is far greater than Lord Rama's. Her sacrifices and struggles are exemplary. Women are creators, and those of you who have built enterprises by overcoming challenges are also role models," Shivakumar said.Shivakumar pitches women’s leadership, entrepreneurshipThe chief minister said women’s leadership was needed at every level of governance and reiterated the state government’s commitment to empowering them.He said women had long been creators, problem-solvers and decision-makers, managing families and resources while also building businesses."When their creativity, capability and determination are supported with access to capital, technology and markets, there is no limit to what they can build," he said, adding that it was the government's responsibility to create an ecosystem where their potential could flourish.Stressing his faith in youth and women, Shivakumar highlighted the Congress government’s five guarantee schemes — Shakti, Gruha Lakshmi, Gruha Jyothi, Anna Bhagya and Yuva Nidhi."Under the Shakti scheme, women travel free across the state in government buses. It has boosted their confidence and self-reliance. The BJP and Prime Minister Narendra Modi had opposed the guarantee schemes. Under Gruha Lakshmi, 1.22 crore women in the state receive Rs 2,000 each, which has helped them manage their families," he said.He also referred to women-centric government programmes, including four per cent interest loans, subsidies and the Stree Shakti scheme, and noted that women account for 40% of doctors graduating every year."You are not confined to the kitchen," he said.‘Women nurture and create leaders’Shivakumar said the Ubuntu initiative had brought together thousands of women with entrepreneurial ambitions and praised them for balancing family responsibilities with their professional lives.According to its website, the Ubuntu Consortium brings together women entrepreneurs’ associations from across India to create an inclusive nationwide network.The chief minister also spoke about changing attitudes towards women and children."In Indian society, there is still a mindset that the first child should be a boy. We must move away from this. As parents, we must teach our children values and discipline. My daughter is an empowered woman who has successfully balanced family and business," he said.Calling women the "eyes of the family" in Indian culture, Shivakumar praised women entrepreneurs for overcoming financial challenges and assured them of government support.He cited Congress leader Sonia Gandhi as an example of resilience, referring to the deaths of her mother-in-law, former prime minister Indira Gandhi, and husband, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi."Although she had two opportunities to become prime minister, she chose to let economist Manmohan Singh take the post. This is an example of the sacrifices women make. Women nurture and create leaders," he said.He also referred to Draupadi and Kunti from the Mahabharata while speaking about women’s talent and potential."We have accepted women's reservation cutting across party lines. Women's leadership is needed from gram panchayats to Parliament. With 33 per cent reservation, it will not be possible to prevent women from becoming leaders," he said.Shivakumar backs Bengaluru tunnel projectShivakumar also urged women entrepreneurs to support the proposed tunnel project aimed at easing traffic congestion in Bengaluru, calling opposition to it "politically motivated."He said the city was expanding rapidly and now had 1.4 crore vehicles, while the government was spending Rs 1.5 lakh crore on infrastructure to strengthen Bengaluru’s transport system.He urged women entrepreneurs not to lose confidence and called on them to contribute to Karnataka’s development."India's development depends on the development of South India. Coming together is the beginning, growing together is progress, and working together is success. Everyone should become a partner in Karnataka's development," he added.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Operation Sindoor commander Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra selected as Ram temple Trust’s first CEO
articles.summary: India News: LUCKNOW: Retired Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who played a key role in commanding air operations during Operation Sindoor, has been selected as the f.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Retired Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who played a key role in commanding air operations during Operation Sindoor, has been selected as the first Chief Executive Officer of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust, on Wednesday.The decorated former Indian Air Force commander retired in April 2026 and will now oversee the temple Trust’s expanding administrative responsibilities.He was among the senior military commanders recognised for leadership during Operation Sindoor. President Droupadi Murmu conferred the Sarvottam Yudh Seva Medal on him in recognition of his distinguished service during the operation.The medal is awarded for the highest order of distinguished service during war, conflict or hostilities. It remains one of India’s rarest military decorations. Mishra’s appointment brings to the Trust a senior leader with extensive experience in operational planning, coordination, logistics and managing large formations.Also read | Ram Mandir’s first CEO has a war command pedigree: Meet Air Marshal Jitendra MishraIn a recent podcast interview, Mishra spoke about the air campaign during Operation Sindoor and explained how Indian forces identified and struck targets deep inside Pakistan. He described how a target located around 314 km away was destroyed after a brief operational instruction to “shoot”.While discussing the operation, he highlighted the importance of planning, precision, technology and coordination among different arms of the armed forces. Several operational details, however, remain classified.Mishra has roots in Uttar Pradesh. He originally belongs to Bhopatpura in Deoria district, around three hours by road from Ayodhya. He comes from a middle-class family and his father was a lecturer.As CEO, Mishra is likely to oversee day-to-day administration, pilgrim facilities, financial arrangements, staff coordination, security-related coordination and the management of large religious events.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1970s, actor Robert Stack owned California acreage that included a private game preserve; his unusual landholding offered a glimpse into Hollywood's forgotten ranch culture
articles.summary: US News: In the 1970s, while Robert Stack was already a familiar face on American television, the actor owned an unusual piece of California real estate far re.
articles.body: In the 1970s, while Robert Stack was already a familiar face on American television, the actor owned an unusual piece of California real estate far removed from Hollywood's studio lots and city life. Stack had acreage in the Sacramento area that included a private game preserve and duck club, according to a 1971 United Press International report. The property was not simply a celebrity retreat acquired for prestige. It had been part of Stack's family for decades, with his father purchasing it in 1925 and later leaving it to Robert and his brother Jim. Stack had grown up hunting there and remained closely connected to the property as an adult. His landholding also reflected a broader chapter in Hollywood history, when stars accumulated ranches, farms and rural retreats across California and the American West.Robert Stack's unusual California landholdingThe 1971 UPI report placed Stack among a generation of Hollywood figures who owned substantial ranches and farmland outside the entertainment capital. While the article discussed celebrities who acquired land for investment, retirement or recreation, it specifically said Stack owned acreage in the Sacramento area that included a game preserve and duck club. The property gave the actor access to hunting grounds away from Los Angeles and reflected an interest that had been part of his life since childhood. Rather than being a piece of land purchased simply as a status symbol, the preserve had a family history and a practical purpose tied to Stack's enthusiasm for hunting and shooting sports.Stack's connection to the Sacramento-area property stretched back decades before his television fame. A 1963 profile published in Guns Magazine reported that his father purchased the property in 1925 and eventually left it to Robert and his brother Jim Stack. The brothers continued to own the land, with Stack saying they intended to keep it in the family so their children could enjoy it as they had. He also recalled beginning to hunt there when he was only seven years old. The detail adds a personal dimension to what might otherwise appear to be an unusual celebrity landholding. The property was not something Stack suddenly acquired after becoming famous. It was part of his family's life and had been associated with him since childhood.The property was near Colusa in the Sacramento ValleyThe 1963 profile identified Stack's private duck club as being near Colusa in California's Sacramento Valley, an area known for wetlands and migratory waterfowl. The magazine described the property as a place where Stack could pursue his passion for duck hunting, with ducks, pheasants and other game birds present on the land. Hunting was carried out according to established seasons and regulations. The location was a world away from the Hollywood environment in which Stack spent much of his professional life. Instead of film sets and television studios, the property offered open countryside, wildlife and the kind of outdoor recreation that had interested him from an early age.Stack was a serious competitive shooterHis interest in the property was closely connected to a much broader passion for shooting sports. Stack was not simply an actor who occasionally went hunting. He became a highly accomplished competitive skeet shooter, earning recognition at national and international levels. A 1963 Guns Magazine profile detailed his achievements and described how his acting career increasingly limited the amount of time he could devote to competition. Even as his Hollywood workload grew, however, shooting and hunting remained important interests. His private duck club therefore fitted naturally into a lifestyle that combined entertainment with serious outdoor pursuits.Hollywood stars were buying ranches and farmlandStack's property was part of a much wider phenomenon. The 1971 UPI report described numerous Hollywood stars who had acquired substantial amounts of land across California and the American West. Bob Hope, Bing Crosby, Jimmy Stewart, Randolph Scott, Jim Nabors, Buddy Ebsen, Jim Arness, Joel McCrea and other actors were among the celebrities associated with ranches, farms or large rural holdings. Their motivations varied. Some treated land as an investment, while others planned to retire there, farm it, raise livestock or simply use it as a private escape. The report provides a snapshot of a period when Hollywood wealth could translate into vast stretches of countryside rather than only expensive homes in Los Angeles.Rural land offered an escape from HollywoodThe attraction of these properties went beyond financial value. For celebrities living under intense public attention, rural land provided privacy and a chance to pursue interests away from cameras and crowds. The 1971 report noted that some stars purchased land specifically as a refuge from city life, while others saw it as a long-term investment. The contrast between Hollywood and the countryside was significant. A star could spend the week working on film or television productions in Los Angeles and then retreat to a ranch, farm or hunting property surrounded by open land. Stack's duck club represented precisely this kind of alternative world, allowing him to return to an environment associated with his childhood and sporting interests.Stack's property was rooted in family rather than fameThe family history makes Stack's landholding different from the stereotypical image of a celebrity buying an enormous estate after achieving success. His father had acquired the property decades earlier, and Stack inherited it with his brother. The actor's memories of hunting there as a child suggest that the land was part of his identity long before he became one of Hollywood's recognisable faces. His reported desire to preserve the property for the next generation also points towards a sense of family continuity. In that respect, the game preserve was less a symbol of Hollywood excess than an inherited piece of countryside that had remained connected to the Stack family for decades.Stack was also linked to a much larger California ranchStack had another documented connection to a major California property, although it should not be confused with his Sacramento-area duck club. In 1990, the Los Angeles Times reported that El Rancho Tajiguas, a roughly 3,600-acre ranch near Santa Barbara, had been owned at different times by Danny Kaye, Robert Stack, Robert Mitchum and John Travolta. The property included a nearly 200-year-old house as well as extensive agricultural land growing avocados, persimmons, oranges, lemons, peaches, plums, figs and cherimoyas. The report shows that Stack's relationship with substantial California land extended beyond the hunting property associated with his family.A forgotten chapter of Hollywood's ranch cultureWhat makes Stack's story particularly revealing is the larger culture surrounding celebrity landownership during the middle of the 20th century. Hollywood stars could accumulate rural properties that served as working farms, cattle ranches, hunting retreats or investments, creating private worlds far removed from the glamour of Los Angeles. The 1971 UPI report captured this trend at a time when many of those properties were still active parts of celebrities' lives. Stack's game preserve was therefore not an isolated curiosity. It was one example of a broader relationship between Hollywood fame and California's countryside, when successful actors often used their wealth to acquire land rather than confining their fortunes to urban real estate.The actor had a life far beyond the screenStack became famous for playing Eliot Ness in The Untouchables and later reached another generation of viewers as the host of Unsolved Mysteries. Yet his life away from the screen included competitive shooting, duck hunting and a longstanding connection to family land in Northern California. The Sacramento-area property helps reveal a side of Stack that was largely invisible to television audiences. Behind the Hollywood actor was a lifelong sportsman who had inherited a piece of California countryside and continued to use it for the activities he had enjoyed since childhood.A private game preserve that captured a vanished eraRobert Stack's California landholding offers more than an unusual footnote to his biography. It provides a glimpse into a period when Hollywood success could lead not only to mansions and celebrity estates but also to ranches, farms and private hunting grounds scattered across the American West. Stack's family had acquired his Sacramento-area property in 1925, he had hunted there since childhood, and by the 1970s it was being reported as acreage containing a game preserve and duck club. That combination of family inheritance, outdoor recreation and celebrity wealth reflects a form of Hollywood life that has become increasingly difficult to imagine.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'You have 18 days and 44 minutes': US brewery's message to the thief who stole its truckload of beer
articles.summary: Tech News News: A US beer company has given a thief 18 days and 44 minutes to return a truckload of stolen beer. According to a BBC report, Pabst Brewing Company said.
articles.body: A US beer company has given a thief 18 days and 44 minutes to return a truckload of stolen beer. According to a BBC report, Pabst Brewing Company said around 40,000 pounds (18,144kg) of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer, worth about $25,000, was stolen from a distribution centre in California after someone allegedly used fake documents to collect the shipment. The company has now turned to social media to try to find the missing beer. "Pabst is officially starting the clock now - you have exactly 18 days and 44 minutes to return our truckload of beer, no questions asked," the company said in the post.Reason behind the unusual '18 days and 44 minutes' deadlineThe unusual deadline is not random. Pabst was founded in 1844, which is why the company chose 18 days and 44 minutes.Pabst said the incident may sound unusual, but stressed that the theft is real. “We realise how ridiculous that sounds, but it's the truth,” the company said in its social media post. “This is real and we are deadly serious.”Pabst also joked about the thief wanting to show off the amount of PBR they had. “STOLEN,” the company announced. “To the thief: we don't fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honourable way.”The brewery also offered an unspecified reward for information that helps recover the shipment.How the beer theft happenedThe stolen beer was being held at an Anheuser-Busch distribution centre in Montclair, California, and was supposed to be delivered to San Diego. According to Montclair police, the alleged thief arrived at the facility with fraudulent paperwork and managed to collect the shipment.A spokesperson said the person who collected the beer was not the driver or person who was supposed to pick up the shipment.“What we discovered was it was just a bad actor essentially who came in and pretended to be the person who was supposed to pick up the beer,” the spokesperson told CBS News.“It wasn't the person who was supposed to pick up the beer and then they drove off with it.”Police said another shipment worth around $45,000 and headed for Tucson, Arizona, was picked up earlier on 17 August. However, it had still not reached its destination two weeks later. About an hour after that incident, the shipment of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer was collected using fraudulent documents.Police are investigating whether the two incidents were connected. “Investigators identified similarities between the two incidents,” police said. “Information provided regarding the trucking company, driver and vehicles involved contained discrepancies and is currently being investigated.”Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: In 2019, a New York couple bought a $1.825M Ridge home for their bearded Collie; after spending another $2M on renovations, ‘Buster’s Retreat’ is now listed for $2.9M
articles.summary: Real Estate News: When Howard and Suze Rubin, both 77, left their warm and cosy home in Florida for New York, they weren’t looking for a high-flying life in NYC. In fac.
articles.body: When Howard and Suze Rubin, both 77, left their warm and cosy home in Florida for New York, they weren’t looking for a high-flying life in NYC. In fact, they moved to NYC for the weather. But they weren’t the ones chasing the cooler weather; their beloved dog, a bearded Collie named Buster, was. Florida may have a lot of beaches, but the sun wasn’t something good boy Buster could handle. “Summer is warm here, and you can’t really go out and play,” Howard told the Wall Street Journal. So the couple bought a home in NYC and spent nearly $3 million on renovating it before listing it on the market.A $3 million home built for one good boyHoward, a technology consultant and professor emeritus of computer science at Hunter College, and Suze, a retired veterinary technician, school psychologist and volunteer EMT, lived in Boca Raton, Florida. But the weather wasn’t suitable for their beloved dog, Buster. So they decided to move. In 2019, the couple purchased a $1.825 million home in Pound Ridge, New York. The home sits on 2.76 acres. Built in 1996, the 5,000 sq. ft. mid-century modern home came with four bedrooms. This may sound solid for a couple, but it was not quite the comfortable home they wanted for Buster, who needed protection from heat and the kind of outdoor space that lets a large dog be, well, a dog! So they invested every penny to make sure their new home, ‘Buster’s Retreat’, was perfect enough for their pooch.The couple spent another $2 million on renovations. They added two sun shelves to the swimming pool—not for themselves, but for Buster to lounge on. “He loves water, but he doesn’t swim,” Howard told the outlet. He has never been in the pool himself. “We never use it. It’s his.” They also added a composite pool deck that deflects heat to protect Buster’s paws. “We don’t want his little feet to get burned,” Howard said. One of Buster’s favourite pastimes is lying on the deck and watching landscapers work when they come over.The pool isn’t the only place dogs like to explore. They feel most at home doing zoomies in the backyard. So the backyard became a landscape architecture project with a single client in mind! They strategically planted Japanese maples throughout the backyard to provide shade coverage. Several large umbrellas were also placed, so Buster “always has protection for his fuzzy body.”A fenced-in area functions as his personal playground. There’s artificial turf where needed. Every element was chosen with the understanding that a bearded Collie’s comfort isn’t negotiable when you’ve committed this deeply. “It is like a party all day for him,” Howard added.There is entertainment available for him indoors as well. When he gets bored with the activities outdoors, he would move to the living room to watch some TV! “He loves to watch a show called Paw Patrol,” Howard said. There are two guest rooms in the house, which are practically Buster’s extra rooms.The couple treated the project with the precision you’d expect from someone in his field. Details matter. Dog paw comfort matters. Everything matters. For a dog that most people would consider spoiled rotten, Buster seems to have settled into his role with appropriate confidence. His humans do not consider it a sacrifice. They do these things with utmost joy. “I wouldn’t say we’ve given up part of our life for him, but we’ve changed our life for him,” Howard said.Buster’s Retreat is back on the marketThough the family of three deeply enjoyed their New York life, Suze began to miss Florida. They are now planning to return to the Sunshine State and have listed the multi-million-dollar home on the market.Sally Slater, the listing agent from Douglas Elliman, doesn’t expect the home to linger. Well, Buster’s Retreat has everything a dog parent can think of: the renovations, the custom landscaping, the pool with its sun shelves, the fenced playground, the temperature-controlled environment. It’s move-in ready, which in real estate language means someone else is about to inherit a home built to exceedingly specific standards!“People are willing to pay a premium for turnkey properties,” Slater said. This could be any pet parent’s dream home.Do you know someone who would be more than happy to buy this perfect home for their beloved dog?
