articles.title: A 50,000-square-foot Gilded Age mansion was bought for $26 million by a convicted fraudster; now the estate is being sold to help settle a $1 billion bankruptcy
articles.summary: US News: A 50,000-square-foot Gilded Age mansion in Mahwah, New Jersey, has become one of the most striking assets caught up in the billion-dollar bankruptcy o.
articles.body: A 50,000-square-foot Gilded Age mansion in Mahwah, New Jersey, has become one of the most striking assets caught up in the billion-dollar bankruptcy of convicted fraudster Miles Guo. The historic ‘Crocker-McMillin mansion,’ built in 1907 for railroad heir ‘George Crocker,’ was purchased by Guo for $26 million in 2021, only months before his financial troubles and criminal case would place his collection of luxury assets under intense scrutiny. Now, the 75-room estate is on the market for $19 million, with the proceeds expected to address the enormous debts linked to Guo’s bankruptcy. According to Business Insider, the mansion’s story stretches from Gilded Age wealth and lavish parties to its seizure in a modern financial scandal. According to Realtor, repeated price cuts have brought the asking price well below both its original listing price and what Guo paid for the property.The 50,000-square-foot Gilded Age mansion at the centre of a billion-dollar bankruptcyThe Crocker-McMillin mansion sits about 25 miles from New York City and overlooks New Jersey's Ramapo Mountains. According to Business Insider, the vast property contains 75 rooms and around 50,000 square feet of living space, making it a remarkable survivor from America's Gilded Age. The mansion was built for George Crocker, the son of Central Pacific Railroad co-founder Charles Crocker. Construction began in 1902 and took five years to complete, costing around $2 million at the time. Architect James Brite designed the house after ‘Bramshill,’ a historic English country estate dating back to the early 1600s. The result was an enormous home built with red brick, carved limestone, steel beams and concrete floors. Its interiors were filled with elaborate wood and marble carvings, while the two-storey Great Hall became the centrepiece of the property. As reported by Business Insider, the hall features a huge fireplace, coffered ceilings and Tiffany silver chandeliers. Perhaps its most unusual feature is a 30-foot Aeolian player pipe organ that still stands in the Great Hall. The instrument could play music automatically using perforated paper rolls, allowing guests to enjoy performances even if nobody in the room knew how to play the organ.Miles Guo brought the mansion into a modern financial scandalThe mansion's latest chapter began when Miles Guo, also known as ‘Ho Wan Kwok’ and ‘Guo Wengui,’ bought the property for $26 million in 2021. According to Business Insider, the home was later seized in connection with his bankruptcy after he was convicted of federal fraud and racketeering conspiracy charges. Realtor reported that prosecutors said Guo spent around $18 million on renovations after buying the mansion. Among the expensive plans were a separate wing for his wife and luxury furnishings that included a $62,000 television, a $53,000 fireplace accessory and Chinese and Persian rugs valued at nearly $1 million. The estate's eight-car garage was also used to store a custom-built Bugatti that cost around $4.4 million. The mansion became one of several high-value assets connected to Guo's bankruptcy and fraud case. Realtor reported that his assets were being sold to help recover money connected to the wider financial collapse, which involved debts and claims worth billions of dollars.A home built for extraordinary wealth and entertainmentWhen the mansion was first completed, it stood on a far larger estate of roughly 1,100 acres. Today, the property has been reduced to 12 acres, but it still retains many of the features associated with its past. Business Insider reported that the original estate included woodlands, a lily pond, Japanese cherry trees and a lake stocked with thousands of trout. Crocker also kept horses on the property, where they could train and race along a private track. Inside, the mansion was designed to accommodate both its owner and his guests. It had 21 bedrooms, a grand dining room, a richly decorated library and a billiards hall. There were also 15 rooms for servants on the third floor. The house was technologically advanced for its time. It had electric-powered heating, laundry machines, a central vacuum system, lifts, a telephone switchboard and even ice cream freezers. Yet George Crocker had little time to enjoy the enormous home. He moved into the mansion in 1907 but died of stomach cancer in 1909, at the age of 54.How did the mansion pass through different handsThe estate changed owners several times over the following decades. In 1912, banker and philanthropist ‘Emerson McMillin’ purchased the property for $1 million. He and his family hosted parties and community gatherings there until his death in 1922. The mansion later came close to becoming a golf and country club before eventually being purchased by the ‘Archdiocese of Newark.’ According to Business Insider, it became home to the ‘Immaculate Conception Seminary,’ with its first group of seminarians moving in during 1927. The Great Hall was converted into a chapel, demonstrating how dramatically the purpose of the mansion had changed from its original days as a private retreat. Over time, however, the property fell into disrepair. It was later restored, helping preserve many of its historic architectural details and transforming it once again into a grand private residence.The mansion is now back on the marketThe Crocker-McMillin mansion was initially listed for $33 million in January 2025. However, Realtor reported that a series of price reductions eventually brought the asking price down to $19 million in December of that year. That figure is $7 million less than the $26 million Guo paid for the estate in 2021. The difference becomes even more striking when the renovation spending is considered. Despite its troubled recent history, the property itself remains an extraordinary piece of American architecture. Its historic interiors still include hand-carved details, murals, marble work and the towering Aeolian organ. Modern features include spaces for entertainment and relaxation while preserving much of the mansion's original grandeur. The house that once symbolised the immense fortunes of the Gilded Age has now become part of a very different story. Its sale is tied not to the expansion of another fortune, but to the effort to settle the financial consequences of a billion-dollar bankruptcy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Not democratically elected’: SC says Manan Kumar Mishra only ‘pro tem’ BCI chairman till fresh election
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said Bar Council of India (BCI) chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra was only a “pro tem Chairman” until a freshly.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said Bar Council of India (BCI) chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra was only a “pro tem Chairman” until a freshly constituted BCI elects its office-bearers, and directed that major policy decisions be taken in consultation with the Attorney General for India and the Solicitor General, who are permanent ex-officio BCI members.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said Mishra could oversee the BCI's day-to-day functioning but could not be treated as a democratically elected office-bearer once the newly elected state bar councils complete the process of constituting a fresh BCI.“You should also bear in mind that you are like a pro tem chairman till a fresh election of the Bar Council of India, pursuant to the elections already conducted in the state bar councils, takes place,” Justice Bagchi told senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar, appearing for the BCI chairman, according to LiveLaw.“So, it is not a situation where he is democratically elected and continues to be so. His term is co-terminus with the elections which are imminent,” the judge said.The court said the existing arrangement could continue for routine administrative work but stressed that institutional checks would apply to policy decisions.“In such situations, day-to-day functioning can be left to the existing arrangement. However, when a policy decision is taken, the participation of a permanent ex officio member acting independently, such as the Attorney General, is necessary,” Justice Bagchi remarked orally, PTI said.The bench also said it was not endorsing Mishra's continued tenure.“We are not placing any stamp of approval upon the existing arrangement. It is apparent that the present chairperson can continue only until a fresh election to the Bar Council of India takes place pursuant to the state bar council elections already conducted,” it said.The observations came while the court heard pleas challenging Mishra's continued occupation of the BCI chairperson's post and the legal basis for extending his tenure until 2030.Senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the petitioners, said Mishra was unanimously elected chairman for a term from April 17, 2025 to April 16, 2030. She also challenged a resolution extending the tenure of the chairman and vice-chairman from three years to five years despite rules prescribing a two-year term.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for one of the petitioners, questioned the creation of the Bar Council of India Trust for Promotion of Education, Legal and Professional Reforms and Improvement in Research.Sankaranarayanan alleged that its deed made 11 managing trustees “original and permanent trustees”. The bench questioned how elected members could appoint themselves as perpetual trustees.“The Bar Council of India is a juristic entity. That entity has created a trust from its assets through the elected members who constituted the Council. Can those elected members make themselves permanent trustees of those assets when the composition of the corporate entity that settled the trust is itself determined through elections?” it asked.The court directed the newly constituted state bar councils to elect their office-bearers and representatives to the BCI within three weeks of notification of their composition. The matter will be heard next on September 23.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2013, Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen put $7 million into counting Africa's elephants; the two-year survey found just 352,271 across 18 countries and exposed a devastating decline
articles.summary: US News: In 2013, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist Paul G Allen committed $7 million to one of the largest efforts ever undertaken to determine how many.
articles.body: In 2013, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist Paul G Allen committed $7 million to one of the largest efforts ever undertaken to determine how many African elephants remained in the wild. Known as the Great Elephant Census, the project was led by Elephants Without Borders and involved scientists, conservation organisations, pilots and wildlife authorities across the continent. Aerial surveys were conducted between 2014 and 2016 across 18 countries, producing an estimate of 352,271 savanna elephants. More alarming than the total was what the census revealed about their decline. In 15 countries where reliable historical comparisons were possible, savanna elephant numbers had fallen by about 30% between 2007 and 2014, with researchers estimating that populations were continuing to decline at roughly 8% each year.Paul Allen's $7 million investment launched a continent-wide countAllen announced the Great Elephant Census in December 2013 after becoming increasingly concerned about the lack of reliable, standardised information on Africa's elephant populations. The initiative was funded with $7 million from his philanthropic organisation and was designed to provide conservationists with a consistent baseline of elephant numbers across much of Africa. Elephants Without Borders led the project, working with a network of conservation organisations and researchers. At the time, it was described as the largest coordinated survey of African savanna elephants since the 1970s. The purpose was not simply to produce a headline figure but to establish where elephant populations were concentrated, where they were declining and where conservation resources were most urgently needed.Scientists surveyed 18 countries from the airThe census used standardised aerial survey methods to count elephants across 18 African countries. Survey teams flew systematic transects over large areas, recording live elephants and elephant carcasses and collecting information that could later be compared across countries. The project involved 90 scientists, six major NGO partners and numerous local researchers, pilots and wildlife officials. Teams used 81 aircraft and flew approximately 294,517 kilometres of survey transects, spending about 9,700 hours in the air. The survey covered approximately 218,238 square kilometres, representing about 24% of the areas included in the study. The scale was intended to make the resulting estimates more consistent and scientifically robust than fragmented counts carried out using different methods.The 352,271 figure covered savanna elephantsWhen the results were published in 2016, researchers estimated that 352,271 savanna elephants were living across the 18 countries included in the census. The estimate had a statistical standard error of 9,085, with a 95% confidence interval of approximately 334,464 to 370,078 elephants. The census was estimated to have accounted for at least 93% of the savanna elephants in those countries. This distinction is important because the figure does not represent every African elephant. The study focused on savanna elephants, which can be surveyed more effectively from aircraft than forest elephants living beneath dense tropical vegetation. The researchers therefore presented the result as a comprehensive assessment of the savanna elephant populations covered by the project rather than a complete count of every elephant on the continent.The real shock was a 30% population declineThe census revealed a far more serious situation than the headline population figure alone suggested. In the 15 countries where sufficient historical data existed for comparison, researchers estimated that savanna elephant numbers had declined by approximately 30% between 2007 and 2014. That represented an estimated loss of around 144,000 elephants during the period. Researchers also estimated that populations were continuing to decline at roughly 8% per year, with poaching identified as the main driver of the decline. The findings showed that the crisis was not limited to a handful of isolated areas. Large-scale losses were occurring across multiple elephant populations, threatening the long-term survival of one of Africa's most iconic species.Poaching emerged as the dominant threatThe researchers linked much of the decline to the illegal killing of elephants for ivory. The survey recorded both living elephants and carcasses, allowing scientists to assess mortality patterns across the surveyed landscapes. High proportions of carcasses in several areas indicated substantial levels of recent elephant deaths, while the geographical pattern of the declines corresponded with regions experiencing serious poaching pressure. The researchers concluded that poaching was the primary factor driving the observed decline in savanna elephant numbers. The findings arrived during a period of intense international concern over the illegal ivory trade, which had created strong incentives for organised poaching in parts of Africa.Protected areas were not always enoughOne of the census's important findings was that most of the elephants counted were already within areas designated for protection. Approximately 84% of the elephants surveyed were inside protected areas, while 16% were outside them. Yet elephant carcasses were still found in protected landscapes, showing that legal protection alone did not necessarily guarantee safety. Rangers and wildlife authorities needed adequate resources to prevent poaching and respond to organised ivory trafficking. The results therefore highlighted the difference between having a protected area on a map and having the capacity to effectively protect wildlife within it.Some elephant populations were holding steadyThe census did not produce uniformly negative results. Researchers found populations that were stable or increasing in several locations, demonstrating that effective conservation could make a measurable difference. Countries and regions including South Africa, Uganda, Kenya and parts of Malawi provided examples of populations that were doing better than those experiencing severe declines. The survey also documented elephant populations in Ethiopia and Kenya that had not been included in some earlier assessments and identified elephants in an area of Botswana where they had previously been thought to have disappeared. These findings were important because they showed conservationists not only where the crisis was most severe but also where management and protection appeared to be producing more positive outcomes.Botswana contained the largest surveyed populationThe census revealed a highly uneven distribution of savanna elephants across the countries surveyed. Botswana accounted for about 37% of the elephants counted, while Zimbabwe accounted for roughly 23% and Tanzania about 12%. Together, those three countries contained a substantial proportion of the animals included in the census. The information was valuable because conservationists could use it to understand where the continent's remaining large populations were concentrated and how those populations compared with areas experiencing rapid declines. Knowing where elephants were most abundant also helped highlight the importance of protecting major strongholds while preventing isolated populations from disappearing.The census created a baseline for future conservationOne of the project's most important achievements was establishing a much stronger baseline for monitoring elephant populations. Before the Great Elephant Census, information came from surveys of different ages and used different methodologies, making comparisons difficult. By using a broadly standardised aerial approach across multiple countries, the census provided a reference point against which future population changes could be assessed. Conservationists could now ask whether elephant numbers in a particular region were increasing, remaining stable or declining, rather than relying solely on estimates or isolated observations. The resulting dataset therefore became a practical conservation tool, helping researchers and authorities identify population trends and determine where anti-poaching and habitat-protection measures were most urgently required.Allen's investment changed what conservationists could seeThe $7 million investment had significance beyond the number of elephants ultimately recorded. It allowed conservationists to undertake a coordinated survey on a scale that would have been difficult to finance through individual national programmes alone. The census exposed the difference between perceived abundance and measured population trends, providing evidence that many savanna elephant populations were declining far faster than previously understood. By combining population counts, carcass observations and historical comparisons, researchers could identify areas where elephants were disappearing most rapidly. In that sense, Allen's contribution helped turn elephant conservation into a more data-driven effort, giving governments and conservation organisations information they could use to target limited resources.The findings became a warning for Africa's elephantsThe Great Elephant Census ultimately showed that counting wildlife can itself become a powerful conservation intervention. The project did not directly stop poaching or restore elephant populations, but it revealed the scale and geography of a crisis that had previously been difficult to measure consistently. The estimate of 352,271 savanna elephants provided a continent-wide baseline, while the 30% decline recorded across 15 comparable countries showed how quickly populations were being lost. At the same time, the areas where elephant numbers remained stable demonstrated that effective protection could work. Allen's $7 million investment therefore produced something more valuable than a single population figure. It gave conservationists a clearer picture of where elephants stood, where they were disappearing and where efforts to protect them had the greatest chance of making a difference.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China’s revised defense law paves way for AI and drones to become military assets
articles.summary: China amended its national defense mobilization law for the first time in 16 years, adding provisions to convert AI, drones, and other tech for war.
articles.body:
China has amended its wartime mobilization law to include advanced technologies like AI systems and drones, aiming to convert civilian infrastructure into military capability during a crisis.

The revised law, passed by China's top legislature, broadens the definition of advanced technologies to include cyberspace, AI, unmanned systems, biotechnology, and more, reflecting the evolving nature of modern warfare.

The amendment, influenced by lessons from the Russia-Ukraine conflict, creates a legal framework for China to rapidly mobilize emerging civilian technologies for defense purposes, highlighting the critical role of unmanned, intelligent, and cyber technologies in modern warfare.

China has rewritten a wartime mobilization law for the first time in 16 years. The amendment adds language specifically aimed at converting AI systems, drones, and other emerging technologies into military capability during a crisis. It passed China's top legislature on Friday and takes effect October 1.

The revised text, published by state news agency Xinhua, states that "the state promotes the application of advanced technologies in national defense mobilization and develops national defense mobilization forces in emerging fields." The law itself does not spell out exactly which technologies qualify as "advanced."

Beijing-based military law expert Xie Dan said the amendment refers to cyberspace, AI, and unmanned systems including drones. It also covers the electromagnetic spectrum, surveying and mapping navigation, biotechnology, and maritime, space, and quantum technologies . Xie said the update covers not just the technologies themselves but also the market entities and specialized talent working within these fields. That broader framing suggests the law is designed to reach well beyond hardware alone, extending into the companies and workers developing it.

Analysts said the inclusion would let Beijing rapidly convert emerging civilian and dual-use infrastructure , including AI systems and unmanned platforms, into defense capabilities during wartime. That kind of conversion mechanism did not exist in the law's previous form, which was last written 16 years ago under very different technological conditions.

Xie pointed directly to the Russia-Ukraine conflict as validation for the update. He said it "further validates the critical role of unmanned, intelligent and cyber technologies in modern warfare, reinforcing the necessity of this legislation." That war has repeatedly shown how cheap drones, AI-assisted targeting , and cyber operations can reshape a modern battlefield.

The amendment lands alongside separate research suggesting China's existing drone manufacturing base may struggle to meet wartime demand even with rapid mobilization. A recent study from the Beijing Institute of Technology found that Chinese factories could fulfill only around 60 percent of projected wartime drone orders. That held true even under an AI-optimized mobilization strategy, due to persistent supply chain constraints around core components.

The law's first version dates back 16 years, reflecting how significantly the technological landscape shaping modern warfare has shifted since then. Where the original law focused on mobilizing conventional industrial capacity, the amendment explicitly builds a legal bridge between China's fast-growing commercial technology sectors and its wartime military needs.

The update itself does not deploy any new weapon or capability on its own. Instead, it creates the legal groundwork China would use to convert existing AI models, drone manufacturing lines, and other emerging-technology infrastructure into defense assets if a large-scale conflict required it. Experts say that kind of formalized conversion process has become increasingly central to how modern militaries prepare for war.

articles.title: Woman arrested after allegedly filming jurors in Lindsay Clancy triple-murder trial
articles.summary: US News: A 56-year-old Massachusetts woman was arrested outside Plymouth Superior Court after she was allegedly caught photographing or filming jurors in the L.
articles.body: A 56-year-old Massachusetts woman was arrested outside Plymouth Superior Court after she was allegedly caught photographing or filming jurors in the Lindsay Clancy triple-murder trial, according to reports.Dawn Light of Sutton was placed in handcuffs outside the courthouse at around 3:40 pm Tuesday, The New York Post reported, citing Massachusetts State Police.She is expected to be arraigned Wednesday on a charge of intimidation of a witness, juror or person furnishing information in connection with criminal proceedings.The state police did not confirm whether Light’s arrest was directly connected to the high-profile Clancy trial.However, CBS Boston reporter Kristina Rex, citing sources, reported that a non-media member had been arrested outside the courthouse and was accused of filming jurors. The jurors allegedly noticed the filming.Light’s arrest came as the 12-member jury, comprising nine women and three men, was dismissed for the day after more than 23 hours of deliberations.The panel had informed the judge earlier Tuesday that it was deadlocked but was instructed to continue deliberating.The jury is expected to return Wednesday at 9 am. Legal experts have said a mistrial could be likely if jurors fail to reach a unanimous verdict.Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan — at their Duxbury home on January 24, 2023.Her defence has argued that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and is seeking a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity.Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington has said he would “absolutely” represent her again if the jury remains deadlocked and the case goes to a retrial.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'I was weeping like an old woman for an hour': Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ashamed of supporting Trump, claims his 'Green Card was canceled' without informing him
articles.summary: US News: Brotosh far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos who was deported from the US to the UK on allegations of visa overstay broke his silence on the ordeal.
articles.body: Brotosh far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos who was deported from the US to the UK on allegations of visa overstay broke his silence on the ordeal and said he would challenge the removal. The former fanboy of President said he felt ashamed of once supporting Trump after he underwent the "physical humiliation" at the hands of the ICE agents. "I didn't really understand the physical reality of how institutionalized the brutality is in America. The manner in which they arrest you, they put you in manacles, everybody is arrested like an MS 13 gang member," he said as he appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored Tuesday.Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Trump before he first became US president in 2016. He is a former editor of Breitbart News and later worked to help the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, explore a presidential run in 2024."It was physically degrading. It was frightening. I don't think I've ever been frightened like that before. I was weeping like an old woman for an hour. I wouldn't wish it on anyone," the 41-year-old commentator said.Milo said he had a Green Card, which the administration canceled without informing him. He said they sent the court order to an address where they knew he did not live anymore. He said he is married to an American and got marriage-based Green Card. In 2017, Yiannopoulos got married to a 'mystery man' in Hawaii. Years later, he started calling himself 'ex-gay'."I was put from a detention facility to a correctional facility, every three hours, they were sort of trying to keep ahead of my lawyers...no one would tell me anything. I mean, I know it's designed to be like that, but it was humiliating, and it was disorienting all the rest of it; it was physically degrading. It was frightening," he said during the interview.Social media commentators said Milo deserved all of it as he has supported ICE in the past. Piers Morgan asked him about his past defence of ICE deporting Somalis. "Groups that have rampant criminality. I don't think the British are an especially egregiously violent group of people. The majority of Somalis in Minnesota are connected with fraud," Milo said.The Department of Homeland Security said ICE arrested Milo Yiannopoulos on August 27. "Yiannopoulos legally entered the country on May 14, 2019, through New York City, New York. He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws. Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal," the DHS said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rampage Jackson fires cameraman after heated livestream argument takes shocking turn
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Former UFC star Rampage Jackson found himself in a heated fight of words with his cameraman during a recent livestream. What started as a simple argum.
articles.body: Former UFC star Rampage Jackson found himself in a heated fight of words with his cameraman during a recent livestream. What started as a simple argument quickly became much more serious when both men began talking about each other’s friends and people around them. The tense moment was caught on both Rampage Jackson’s and DeenTheGreat’s livestreams. The argument later turned into a chase, with Jackson running after the cameraman and saying he was fired. The cameraman managed to run away before things could become even more serious.Rampage Jackson’s livestream argument with cameraman gets heatedThe argument started when Jackson and his cameraman began talking about who says more bad things about the other person’s “people.” Jackson then asked the cameraman to give him an example of when he had talked badly about someone.However, the cameraman did not want to continue that part of the conversation and tried to end the discussion. Jackson kept talking and brought up a friend of the cameraman.Jackson said he had helped the friend by getting him a job. The cameraman disagreed with him and said, “You didn't give s*** a job.” He also claimed that Jackson had never really wanted to give his friend work.The exchange became more tense as both men continued arguing. Neither side appeared willing to back down, and the conversation soon moved from a verbal disagreement to a much more heated confrontation.Cameraman’s comment sends Rampage Jackson chasing after himThings took a bigger turn when the cameraman insulted people who were appearing as guests on Jackson’s livestream. The comment clearly made Jackson angry.Jackson then moved toward the cameraman and began chasing him. During the chase, Jackson also told him that he was fired while shouting several angry words at him.The cameraman quickly ran away from Jackson. His speed helped him get out of the situation before the confrontation could become physical.The entire moment was captured during the livestream, giving viewers a close look at how quickly a normal argument can turn into a serious clash.While Jackson appeared extremely angry during the incident, the confrontation did not end with a reported physical fight between the two men. The cameraman got away, while Jackson made it clear that he no longer wanted him working for him.The heated livestream showed a very tense moment between Rampage Jackson and his cameraman. What began as an argument about friends and past comments quickly grew after the cameraman insulted Jackson’s guests. Jackson then chased him and fired him during the confrontation. The cameraman managed to escape, bringing the intense moment to an end before it became a physical fight.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bhotekoshi flood 'serious signal' of rising climate risks, says Nepal PM Shah urging global action
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal PM Balendra Shah on Wednesday described the catastrophic Bhotekoshi River flood of August 26 as a stark warning of escalating climate risks in t.
articles.body: Nepal PM Balendra Shah on Wednesday described the catastrophic Bhotekoshi River flood of August 26 as a stark warning of escalating climate risks in the Himalayan region, urging the international community to share responsibility for tackling the growing impact of climate change.Addressing Parliament, Shah said experts had identified the disaster as one of the largest in the region, as being caused by an avalanche of snow and rock in the high Himalayas. He said the scale of the devastation showed that countries in the Himalayan region were facing increasing risks alongside the effects of climate change.“This is a serious signal that, alongside climate change, the risks we must bear in the Himalayan region are increasing,” Shah said. He called for Nepal to forcefully present before the international community the disasters it is suffering due to climate change.“Climate change is a product of the whole world's contribution; mitigating and managing its effects is the shared responsibility of the global community,” Shah said, stressing the need for international cooperation to address the consequences of a changing climate.Death toll reaches 1,127The flood struck riverside settlements in Rasuwa district on the morning of August 26 and rapidly affected neighbouring areas, including Nuwakot and Dhading. The disaster has left a massive human and economic toll, with 3,916 people still out of contact and 1,127 bodies recovered, according to the latest figures presented by Nepali Police.A total of 11,993 people have been rescued, while 292 injured people were admitted to hospitals, of whom 182 have since been discharged, news agency ANI reported.Climate risks expose Himalayan vulnerabilityThe disaster has also caused extensive damage to critical infrastructure. Eight operating hydropower projects with a combined capacity of 281 MW and four projects under construction with a capacity of 388 MW were damaged, disrupting 431.1 MW of generation capacity.Major sections of the Galchhi-Betrawati-Rasuwagadhi road and the Prithvi Highway were destroyed or heavily damaged, along with 48 suspension bridges and 31 motorable bridges.As search operations continue for those still missing, the disaster has emerged as a stark reminder of the vulnerability of Himalayan communities and infrastructure to increasingly severe climate-related risks.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
